transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-07-21
Start: 14:30 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Liu (Redwood SE), Priya Raman (CTO - Atlas), Carlos Vega (Infra Lead - Atlas), Sophie Tran (Security)

Summary: quick technical deep dive focused on on-prem / air-gapped artifact delivery, GPU driver packaging, and offline licensing for Redwood Private. Discussed runtime performance implications (latency vs throughput), KV cache behavior, batching, quantization tradeoffs, and installation/verification steps for air-gapped envs. Agreed next steps: checklist + hashes, offline license doc, schedule POC benchmark window.

Topics:
- Artifact delivery & offline licensing patterns
- GPU driver / kernel module compatibility, container runtime (nvidia-container-toolkit)
- Runtime performance: batching, KV cache, quantization impacts
- Validation checksums, install verification, approvals and procurement

Transcript:
00:00 Maya: okay, everybody thanks for joining, um we'll, we'll walk through the on-prem air-gapped flow and the points you flagged in the questionnaire. Ethan's gonna cover the driver and runtime details and then we'll hit licensing and the POC steps, sound good?
00:18 Priya: yeah that's perfect, thanks. We do want to focus on the operational steps — how we get artifacts into our secure environment and what proofs you can provide.
00:28 Ethan: great, I'll start with driver and runtime stuff. high level, Redwood Private runs our inference runtime in containers but in air-gapped setups we provide a bundle: drivers, toolkit, the runtime images, plus a checksum manifest and an install script. All of that is signed.
00:45 Carlos: when you say "drivers" are you including the kernel modules? our infra team doesn't allow arbitrary kernel module installs without approval.
00:52 Ethan: yep, we include the NVIDIA driver packages which have the kernel modules; we also provide a pre-validated DKMS flow for common kernels and a fallback pre-built kernel module for the most common enterprise kernels. note: DKMS won't always be allowed in locked-down distros so we have a fallback static module.
01:10 Sophie: how do you verify integrity? we can't accept live downloads or external repos.
01:16 Ethan: we provide a signed tarball plus SHA256 manifest. the manifest is signed by Redwood's offline signing key. we also provide PGP-signed release notes and an integerated verification script you run in your staging air-gapped environment. the script verifies checksums and signature and then unpacks into a staging dir.
01:35 Priya: what's the recommended mechanism for transferring these artifacts — usb, internal repo, or shipment?
01:41 Maya: depends on your internal policies. we commonly provide an S3-compatible offline bundle (on a drive) or a secure USB image with checksums. some customers prefer encrypted hard drives shipped with tamper seals and a shared symmetric key delivered via a separate channel.
01:57 Carlos: ok, we usually prefer controlled media transfer with an internal change request. can you produce a checklist of the exact files and hashes?
02:05 Ethan: yes, that's on the checklist; we'll include file list, size, SHA256, signing cert, and step-by-step for loading images into your private repo.
02:14 Priya: what about the container runtime? we use containerd with the nvidia toolkit, and our kernels are on 5.15.x. any known issues?
02:23 Ethan: containerd + nvidia-container-toolkit is our recommended combo for performance and stability. for kernel 5.15 we've validated our runtime with the NVIDIA driver 535.x and the toolkit 1.11 in our test matrix. if you're on an older driver we'll provide guidance but performance may differ, particularly around CUDA IPC and peer-to-peer which affect KV cache behavior.
02:43 Sophie: KV cache? can you explain how the KV cache interacts with GPU memory and driver versions, because that's a security question for us too — we want to make sure there are no unexpected IPC channels opened.
02:54 Ethan: sure, so KV cache is stored in GPU memory most of the time; the runtime manages it and we use CUDA contexts pinned to the process. the IPC/p2p behaviors depend on driver and kernel versions; mismatched drivers can cause fallback to host memory which increases latency and can also change attack surface. we document recommended driver/kernel combos to avoid that.
03:16 Maya: also, on the subject of security, we can provide a short attestation report showing that the runtime only uses expected kernel modules and that there are no extra daemons. it's not a full SBOM but a runtime module list and signatures.
03:28 Priya: that's helpful.
03:30 Ethan: switching to performance: for latency-sensitive workloads we recommend smaller batch sizes and aggressive KV cache warmup. for throughput you bump batching and enable our automatic batching scheduler. quantization also matters — INT8 quant gives 2-4x throughput improvements depending on model and kernel optimizations but you need validation for quality.
03:53 Carlos: do you provide quantized artifacts or do we quantize in-place?
03:57 Ethan: we can provide both. for air-gapped customers we often ship a quantized model artifact and the conversion tool so you can re-run conversion internally. we also include the calibration seed data set as a small sample for verification.
04:12 Priya: are there licensing constraints for shipping quantized models?
04:15 Maya: depends on the base model license. for Redwood-managed models we have license tiers that allow distribution within customer environments; for third-party models you'll need to comply with their distro license. we'll include a license matrix in the doc.
04:27 Carlos: back to drivers — what about mismatched kernel headers? we run a hardened kernel and sometimes don't have headers installed.
04:35 Ethan: if headers aren't available we fall back to pre-built modules for the most common enterprise kernels. if your kernel is custom we can provide a support path where we build modules from your exact kernel -- that requires sharing a few artifacts (vmlinux or full config) via secure channel and some validation time.
04:55 Sophie: how long does that take? our change window is tight.
04:59 Ethan: typically 2-3 business days for us to produce a validated module if kernels are standard; custom ones can be up to a week. we'll call that out in the checklist as an expected latency.
05:12 Priya: performance numbers — do you have any benchmark we can use as a baseline for our POC? we use Mistral-like models at ~4k context.
05:21 Ethan: yes, we'll share sample benchmark configs. rough numbers: on A100 80GB with optimized kernels and INT8 quant, we see ~X tokens/sec per GPU at batch size 8 for 4k context — i.e., ~ (we'll attach the spreadsheet). note: these are synthetic; your workload will differ. for latency SLOs, with small batch=1 and KV cache warm, tail latency is driven by CUDA memcpy and kernel launch times; those are sensitive to driver version.
05:51 Maya: I'll attach our performance spreadsheet and the recommended perf config for on-prem.
05:57 Carlos: what about offline licensing enforcement? we can't have outbound license checks in an air gap.
06:03 Maya: we support node-locked and node-count licenses. for air-gapped sites we provide an offline license file that is signed and can be verified by the runtime using a bundled public key. there's no outbound call required. we also have a time-limited license flavor that requires periodic re-issuance via secure transfer.
06:20 Sophie: is the license key tied to hardware IDs? we have policies against sending hardware fingerprints out.
06:26 Maya: we can do a handshake both ways: option A: node-locked license tied to a local HSM or TPM attest that you provide internally (we don't receive the hardware fingerprint). Option B: time-limited license that's not tied to hardware but must be refreshed. both approaches avoid live telemetry.
06:41 Priya: any offline audit logs we need to be aware of?
06:44 Ethan: runtime produces signed event logs and we can configure retention locally. for compliance we can also ship a script to scrub any customer-identifiable metadata.
06:52 Carlos: what's in the install bundle? a short list would be great.
06:55 Ethan: bundle includes: driver tarball (NVIDIA drivers), nvidia-container-toolkit package (containerd), runtime containers (redwood-runtime:version), quantized model artifacts (optional), install scripts, sha256 manifest, PGP signature, release notes, and a verification tool.
07:15 Priya: will you provide guidance for offline patching? we will need to patch drivers on our own cadence.
07:20 Ethan: yes, patch guidance and CVE mapping is in the release notes; we also provide back-ported patches for a limited window for LTS kernels.
07:28 Sophie: how do you handle security approvals — do you provide SBOMs for container images?
07:32 Maya: we can provide image SBOMs and signed digests for each image. for air-gapped sites we include the SBOM files in the bundle.
07:40 Priya: any gotchas for NVSwitch or multi-GPU RDMA?
07:44 Ethan: for RDMA/p2p you need matching driver stacks and firmware versions; mismatches can cause remote memcpy fallback and big perf hits. we'll capture that in the checklist as a 'firmware and driver matrix' you must validate before POC.
07:59 Carlos: about installation — will your script try to auto-reboot nodes? our ops team will want manual approval.
08:05 Ethan: the default is no automatic reboot; we surface a dry-run mode that checks kernel module compat and then you can approve.
08:12 Maya: moving to POC timeline: typical flow is: 1) Atlas provides target cluster spec, 2) Redwood ships bundle, 3) Atlas loads into internal repo and runs validation script, 4) Redwood and Atlas run a 48-72 hour benchmark window.
08:26 Priya: that sounds fine; can you give us an example POC acceptance criteria?
08:31 Maya: yes. example: sustained throughput within 15% of expected bench for N hours, tail latency < desired SLO for 95th/99th, and successful install with no kernel module errors across nodes. we can formalize that in the doc.
08:46 Ethan: a couple of implementation notes: 1) KV cache warmup policy is configurable; we can set a static warmup for the POC so you have predictable latency; 2) batching scheduler has backpressure heuristics to protect latency-critical routes; 3) quantization artifacts include a per-layer quality delta report.
09:09 Priya: we need to be careful on quality. have you seen model regressions after quantization?
09:14 Ethan: sometimes, yes. that's why we include per-layer metrics and a small eval set so you can run a quick quality regression check. for many LLMs INT8 is fine but it's model-dependent.
09:26 Carlos: what's the support SLA during the POC? we need fast response for install issues.
09:31 Maya: for POCs we usually provide 24/7 critical support for the benchmark window, with an SE on-call for install problems. support hours and contact list will be in the packet.
09:43 Sophie: in the manifest, do you include signature certs? we'll need root CA details to verify.
09:48 Ethan: yes we include the certificate chain and fingerprints; the verification tool will fail fast if the chain doesn't validate.
09:56 Priya: any performance tuning knobs you recommend out of the box?
09:59 Ethan: enable GPU persistent memory and pinned allocation, tune batch size to 2-8 depending on latency requirements, pre-pin KV cache for hot prefixes, and for multi-GPU use our sharded KV strategy to reduce cross-GPU syncs. we'll send a recommended config yaml.
10:20 Carlos: what about drift detection in offline envs — if we ship a patched runtime how do you ensure it's the same code?
10:26 Ethan: all artifacts are content-addressed with digests; we include a manifest and signed attestations. we can also provide a reproducible build log so you can match commit hashes locally.
10:38 Maya: okay, sounds like consensus on next steps. I'll send the offline licensing doc and the driver checklist; Ethan will produce the install scripts + hashes; we'll propose POC dates.
10:47 Priya: thanks. one last question — will Redwood run any remote profiling that touches our network? we can't have outbound pings.
10:53 Maya: no outbound telemetry required. profiling runs are local; if we need logs we ask you to push them to a secure bucket or provide the artifacts over the secure channel.
11:03 Carlos: great. also please include an escalation path for critical issues.
11:07 Maya: yep. we'll include contact numbers and an on-call roster for SEs during the POC.
11:12 Sophie: can you show an example of the verification output? a small example would be useful.
11:16 Ethan: sure, we'll include a sample verification log in the bundle and an example run in the doc.
11:22 Priya: ok thanks everyone, this was useful.
11:25 Maya: thanks all — we'll follow up with the docs and schedule.

End of transcript.
